1→# Supply Code Jurisprudence — Processing Runbook

Self-contained procedure for processing a batch of judgments into the **lean schema**.
Any session (fresh or resumed) can execute this from repo state alone. Branch:
`claude/supply-code-jurisprudence-design-yiwgen` (git pull first).

## Batch size
**8 cases per run**, with an early stop if cumulative source exceeds ~22,000 words
(protects quality when a long-case cluster appears). Most UP writ orders are short
10→(~1-2k words); the occasional long regulatory/Supreme Court judgment counts more.

## Queue & progress
- Pending = files in `html_input/` (process the HTML format — smaller than the `.mht`
  twin in `input/`, extracts to the same clean text, no quoted-printable edge cases).
- "Next" = alphabetical order in `html_input/`.
- A case is **done** when its `summaries/json/<id>.json` + `summaries/pdf/<id>_<slug>_Digest.pdf`
  are committed and both source twins (`.html` and the `.mht` in `input/`) are moved to `processed/`.
- Ids are `SCJ-0NN`, sequential and stable; see `state/index.json` (`next_seq`).

20→## Per-case flow
1. `python tools/extract_judgment.py "html_input/<name>.html" /tmp/... <id>` → `<id>.txt` + `<id>.fp.json`.
2. Read `<id>.txt` (short cases: main thread is fine). Read `<id>.fp.json` for the Indian Kanoon **doc-ids**.
3. Write `summaries/json/<id>.json` in the lean schema (below). Use ONLY authorities actually
   discussed in the text; match their doc-ids to `<id>.fp.json`; never invent a citation or holding.
4. Render: `python tools/gen_scj.py summaries/json/<id>.json /tmp/<id>.html` then
   `chromium --headless=new --no-sandbox --no-pdf-header-footer --print-to-pdf=summaries/pdf/<id>_<slug>_Digest.pdf file://<abs>/<id>.html`.
5. Add the case to `state/index.json` (status `done`); `git mv` both source twins to `processed/`.

## After the batch
30→- `python tools/build_supply_code.py` — rebuilds `jurisprudence/index.json` (provision- &
  principle-keyed spine + authorities ledger). Never hand-edit that file.
- Commit (one commit for the batch is fine) and `git push -u origin <branch>`.

## Lean schema (per case) — the ONLY thing we keep
Top-level: `case_id, title, neutral_citation, court, bench, coram, date_of_judgment (ISO),
date_display, docket, disposition, headnote, holding_units[], principle_tags[], not_decided[], authorities[]`.

- **headnote**: one dense paragraph stating the whole-case rule (the anchor when a case
  appears under several provision chapters).
40→- **holding_units[]**: `{provision, code, clause, topic, type, question?, holding, limiting_facts?,
  qualifier?, paras, flag?}`. `provision` is the key, e.g. `UP-2005::4.3(f)`, `EA2003::56(2)`,
  `WB-2004::5.2` (multi-state — key by the actual Code/Act, never merge a Code clause into an Act
  section). `type` = `"supply_code"` (green) for a Supply Code clause, `"interplay"` (grey) for a
  companion Act provision (s.56(2), s.126/127, s.46, s.174, tariff ss.61/62/64…). `flag` records a
  data-quality note (e.g. a litigant conflating a Code clause with an Act section) or transitional/
  multi-state scope. `paras` = judgment paragraph pins.
- **principle_tags[]**: `{tag, application, lead_authorities:[{name,docid}], paras}` — cross-cutting
  doctrines (kebab-case tag reused across cases): e.g. `own-wrong-maxim`, `arrears-run-with-the-premises`,
  `arrears-bar-is-premises-specific`, `arrears-apportioned-pro-rata-on-subdivision`,
50→  `theft-uue-enforced-via-code`, `first-due-on-billing-not-consumption`,
  `disconnection-barred-but-recovery-not`, `opportunity-before-final-assessment`,
  `relegate-to-statutory-remedy`, `regulator-cannot-change-rules-at-truing-up`.
- **not_decided[]**: `{point, note, docid?, paras}` — the negative-authority register (points raised
  but not decided; expressly-reserved questions). Vital so nobody over-reads a case.
- **authorities[]**: `{name, citation, court, docid, proposition, how_treated, how_treated_paras,
  cited_by, treatment}`. Capture **every** precedent the judgment cites — electricity-related or not
  (that master table of citations is a project aim). `cited_by` ∈ {Petitioner, Respondent, Court}.
  `treatment` ∈ {Followed, Approved, Applied, Affirmed, Distinguished, Doubted, Overruled, Referred,
  Relied on}. `proposition` = the abstract rule; `how_treated` = what THIS court did with it (kept
60→  separate on purpose — proposition is reusable across cases, how_treated is case-specific).

Reference records: `SCJ-001` (parallel-operating charges; own-wrong maxim; s.56(2) interplay),
`SCJ-008` (full vested-right-of-appeal authority chain), `SCJ-009` (leading s.56(2) authority).

## Scope notes
- The corpus is **multi-state** (U.P. 2005 is the bulk, but Delhi/DERC, West Bengal 2004, Rajasthan
  etc. appear). Key provisions by their actual Code/Act.
- Theft (s.126 UUE / s.135) cases belong in the jurisprudence: the Supply Code supplies the
  assessment/compounding machinery. Even a "thin" case is a node — record it, don't discard it.
70→- Supreme Court / APTEL judgments that surface in the supply-code search are kept; set `court` accurately.

- **Finding a case from a name/citation alone.** The user gave a case name + SCC citation, no file, no doc-id. `extract_judgment.py` cannot search — it only fetches a known doc-id. Instead, hit the IK **search** endpoint directly with the same token: `curl -sS -X POST "https://api.indiankanoon.org/search/?formInput=<url-encoded query>&pagenum=0" -H "Authorization: Token $IK_API_TOKEN"`. Relevance is weak on generic multi-word queries (lots of noise); narrow to the most distinctive party-name fragment, and a `doctypes:supremecourt`-style filter helps. - **A judgment can block-quote another case at such length that the quoted case's own paragraph numbers appear inline and collide with the citing judgment's numbering.** SC-002 has two unrelated "¶51"s in its raw text — the real one (about §126/§127), and one from an unrelated debt-recovery judgment it quotes for an interpretive canon. 1→# Supply Code Jurisprudence

Goal: turn ~300 High Court judgments **on the electricity Supply Code** into a single,
navigable body of jurisprudence — not just 300 isolated case notes, but a spine organised
by *Supply Code provision* and by *legal principle*, so a reader can ask "what have the
courts held about Clause 4.26(e)?" or "how has the 'no advantage of one's own wrong' maxim
been applied to licensees?" and get every case, with its holding and paragraph pins.

This project reuses the existing digest pipeline (`../tools/`, `../high-court/`) and adds one
10→new layer on top: a **provision-keyed jurisprudence index**.

## What we extract from each judgment

Driven by your instinct — *issue → court's reasoning → final decision* — plus what a
jurisprudence needs to be searchable and trustworthy. Per case we capture:

| Field | What it is | Your ask |
|---|---|---|
| `issues[]` | The points for determination, **framed around the Supply Code** where the court frames them | "the issue related to supply code" |
20→| `facts[]` | 2–4 tight paragraphs — only what the holding turns on | "summarised facts" |
| `reasoning[]` | Issue-by-issue: `{point, explanation, paras}` | "court's logic" |
| `ratio` | The binding ratio decidendi, in one paragraph | "court reasoning" (the durable core) |
| `disposition` / `result` | The operative order | "final holdings" / "final decision" |
| `obiter[]` | Notable observations that are *not* the ratio | — |
| `interpretations[]` | Provision-by-provision construction (`{provision, interpretation}`) | (jurisprudence backbone) |
| `significance[]` | Why the case matters, in plain terms | — |
| `authorities[]` | Every case cited, with **treatment** (followed/distinguished/…), proposition, and Indian Kanoon `docid` | "authority cited" |
| **`supply_code`** | **New.** The Supply Code regime + each Supply Code provision construed: `{provision, topic, provision_text, question, holding, treatment, paras}` | the heart of the jurisprudence |
| docket | `neutral_citation`, `court`, `coram`, `date`, `nature`, `parties`, `provisions` | provenance |
30→
Every reasoning/interpretation point carries **paragraph pins** (`paras`) back to the source,
so any statement can be verified against the original at a glance — the same discipline the
existing HC pipeline enforces (`tools/PLAYBOOK.md` §3–4).

`summaries/json/SCJ-001.json` is the fully worked reference case (Indian Oil Corp. v. State of
U.P.). Read it alongside this file — it is the schema, in the concrete.

## Why JSON (your suggestion — kept)

40→JSON is right: it is the machine-readable **source of truth** that powers both the per-case
digest PDF and the cross-case index. One extract, three products:

1. **`summaries/json/<id>.json`** — clean, per-case digest (the leaf).
2. **`summaries/pdf/<id>_<slug>.pdf`** — the human-readable digest, rendered from the JSON.
3. **`jurisprudence/index.json` + `jurisprudence/provisions/*.json`** — the spine, generated by
   folding every case's `supply_code` block together.

## The jurisprudence layer (what makes this more than a pile of summaries)

50→`jurisprudence/index.json` is keyed two ways:

- **By Supply Code provision** (`UP-2005::4.26(e)`, …): every case touching that clause, each
  with its holding, treatment, and pins. This is the "comprehensive jurisprudence on supply
  code" — read a clause, see its entire judicial history.
- **By legal principle** (`no-advantage-of-own-wrong`, `acquiescence-cuts-both-ways`, …): the
  cross-cutting doctrines, with how each case applied them.

`jurisprudence/provisions/<code>-<clause>.json` (optional, for heavily-litigated clauses) is a
per-provision deep file — the full run of holdings on a single clause, chronologically.
60→
A precision rule the worked example already exercises: **State Supply Codes differ** (U.P.
2005, Gujarat 2005, …) and litigants sometimes **conflate a Code clause with an Act section**
(here, "Clause 56(2)" of the Code vs Section 56(2) of the Act). The index keys provisions by
`CODE::clause`, never merging a Code clause into an Act section, and records the conflation as a
`data_quality_note` rather than silently "correcting" it.

## Folders

| Folder | Purpose |
70→|---|---|
| `input/` | Raw judgments awaiting processing (upload here). |
| `processed/` | Sources moved here once the digest is committed (the move *is* the progress marker). |
| `extracts/` | Per-case cleaned text (`.txt`) + fingerprint (`.fp.json`) + structured extract (`.extract.json`). |
| `summaries/json/` | Per-case clean digest JSON (the leaves). |
| `summaries/pdf/` | Per-case digest PDFs (deliverables). |
| `summaries/merged/` | Cross-case compilations (table of authorities, comparative facts, …). |
| `jurisprudence/` | **The spine:** `index.json` (provision- & principle-keyed) + `provisions/`. |
| `state/` | `index.json` (filename → case id), `authorities-ledger.json`. |

80→## Pipeline (per case) — reuses `tools/PLAYBOOK.md`

1. Drop the judgment (PDF / HTML / MHT / Indian Kanoon doc-id) into `input/`.
2. `python tools/extract_judgment.py "<input>" supply-code/extracts <id>` → `.txt` + `.fp.json`.
3. **One Haiku sub-agent** reads the `.txt` and writes `extracts/<id>.extract.json` — including the
   `supply_code` block — never reading the judgment into the main thread.
4. Verify (`tools/verify.py`, extended to check every `supply_code.provisions_construed[].provision`
   actually appears in the text and every pinned paragraph exists).
5. Render the digest PDF; write `summaries/json/<id>.json`; append authorities to the ledger;
   **fold the `supply_code` block into `jurisprudence/index.json`**.
90→6. `git mv` the source into `processed/`; mark the case `done` in `state/index.json`; commit.
7. After each batch: rebuild `jurisprudence/index.json` and the merged compilations; push.

Case ids are `SCJ-0NN` (Supply Code Jurisprudence), sequential and stable.

## Status

`SCJ-001` (Indian Oil Corp. v. State of U.P., 2024:AHC:8729-DB) is drafted end-to-end as the
reference sample. The remaining ~299 judgments are processed in fresh sessions, in batches,
against this schema once it is signed off.

Rs.65,48,861 and compounding fee was quantified as Rs.20,00,000/-.
The petitioner challenged the final assessment dated 05.07.2023 in Writ-
C No.26411 of 2023, which was disposed of on the ground of alternative
remedy of appeal under Section 127 of the Act of 2003. The petitioner
challenged the final assessment in appeal before the respondent no.3,

110→4
WRIC No. - 12783 of 2024
which has been dismissed by the order dated 14.03.2024. Thus
aggrieved, the petitioner is before this Court.
7.
It is contended by the learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner
that under the provisions of Section 135 of the Act of 2003, whoever
dishonestly taps, makes or causes to be made in connection with
overhead, underground or under water lines or cables or service wires or
service facilities of a licencee or supplier, as the case may be, so as to
120→abstract or consume electricity shall be punishable with imprisonment.
Therefore, unless and until electricity is abstracted or consumed or used,
prosecution under Section 135 of the Act cannot be initiated against the
petitioners. The reports prepared by the officials of respondent no.4 on
28.10.2022 and 08.12.2022 does not show that any electricity was being
abstracted, consumed or used by the petitioner, except for the
observation in the report dated 28.10.2022 that there exists possibility of
theft in future. It is further contended that the inspection report dated
17.12.2022 refers possibility of theft through artificial means, however,
neither the petitioner was found consuming electricity, nor there was any
130→artificial means available in the premises of the petitioner, which could
have been used for abstracting or consuming electricity running from the
double pole behind the premises of the petitioner.
8.
Learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner has further stated that in
the absence of any positive act of abstraction or consumption of
electricity by resorting to any artificial means as mentioned in Section
135 of the Act of 2003, the allegation of theft of electricity is not
established, as such, no demand under Section 126 of the Act could have
been made against the petitioner. It is further submitted that even if it is
140→assumed that the petitioner could have abstracted or consumed electricity
with help of artificial means, the assessment of electricity usage as
quantified in the final assessment order dated 05.07.2023 for a period of
365 days is unsustainable, in view of the fact that in the report prepared
by the officials of respondent no.4 on 08.12.2022, there is a clear
observation that no 11KV cable or wire is attached to the double pole

5
WRIC No. - 12783 of 2024
energized line, therefore, possibility of theft, even if accepted, could
150→have been only with effect from 09.12.2022. 
9.
Learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner further argues that in
view of the order passed by the National Green Tribunal, the production
and sale of stone grits was completely banned w.e.f. 22.06.2018. The
stone grits found near the crusher plant was the stock lying with the
petitioner when the crusher plant was abruptly stopped and the petitioner
was directed to suspend his business. He further contends that the entire
proceedings against the petitioner under Section 126 read with Section
135 of the Act of 2003 is on basis of presumption. 
160→10.
Learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner in support of his
contentions has relied upon a Division Bench judgment of this Court in
the case of Ashok Kumar and others vs. State of U.P. and other
reported in 2008 (6) ADJ 660. Paragraph nos.56 to 60 of the aforesaid
judgment are relied upon and are reproduced hereinafter:-
�56. The provisional assessment notices are in question in all these cases
except writ petitions no. 21986 of 2008 and 22356 of 2008 and have also
been challenged on the ground that neither they have been issued
observing the procedure prescribed under Section 126 of the Act, 2007
170→read with Clause 6.8 of Code, 2005 nor the petitioners have been given
adequate opportunity of defence.
57. Sub-section 1 of Section 126 provides that if on inspection, the
assessing authority comes to the conclusion that the person concerned is
indulged in unauthorized user of electricity, the assessing officer shall
provisionally assess, to best of its judgment, electricity charges payable
by that person or by any other person benefited by such use. Therefore,
the conditions precedent to attract the power of assessment under Section
126 (1) is the conclusion drawn by the assessing officer that the person
concerned has indulged in unauthorized use of electricity.
180→58. The term "unauthorized use of electricity" is defined in explanation
(b) to Section 126 which includes usage of electricity (i) by any artificial
means; or (b) by a means not authorised by the concerned person or
authority or licensee; or (iii) through a tampered meter; or (iv) for the
purpose other than for which the usage of electricity was authorised.
Before issuing an assessment notice, therefore, the assessing officer must
record its conclusion that the person concerned or any other person
benefited has used electricity unauthorizedly in terms as defined in
Explanation (b) of Section 126. The Act in respect to the stage of
recording of conclusion by assessing officer regarding user of electricity
190→by the person unauthorizedly does not provide specifically for any
opportunity of hearing to the person concerned but also simultaneously
does not prohibit the same. The allegation of unauthorised use of
electricity by a person concerned, as defined in Explanation (b) also

6
WRIC No. - 12783 of 2024
covers within its ambit certain acts/omission which constitute an offence
under Section 135 of the Act, 2003. Therefore, it is a serious matter and
no person can be indicted and held guilty of user of electricity
200→unauthorizedly unless he is given an opportunity of hearing before
coming to such conclusion. Where a person is held guilty of unauthorised
user of electricity, besides making him responsible for paying penalty in
the shape of assessment under the Act, 2003 it also causes stigma on his
conduct. He is declared an anti-social person indulging in a serious
unsocial activity, by causing loss to the society and country in general and
electricity undertaking in particular. Such condemnation of a person
would not be permissible on the mere vagaries of the authority i.e.
assessing officer unless such a person is given a fair opportunity of
hearing i.e. putting his defence before the said authority. This Court is
210→clearly of the view that before making provisional assessment, the
assessing officer, in law, is bound to afford an opportunity to the
consumer or person concerned of the allegations of means and ways in
which he is said to have unauthorizedly used electricity, and, should be
given an opportunity of placing his defence. Thereafter the assessing
officer shall record its conclusion with respect to unauthorised use of
electricity, to confer upon himself the jurisdiction to issue provisional
assessment notice. The object of opportunity at the two stages namely,
before arriving at the conclusion of unauthorised use of electricity and
before making final assessment are distinct. In the former, it is the very
220→issue whether the consumer is guilty of unauthorised use of electricity or
not and in later case it is the quantum of amount which he is required to
pay as a compensation and a fiscal preventive measure for committing
such irregularity. The first one is the stage of finding the person guilty and
later one is the stage of determining extent of monetary liability for
compensating electrical undertaking qua the alleged unauthorised use of
electricity by such persons. It is only when the proceedings are conducted
in the above manner, the assessment made can be held valid and not
otherwise.
59. It is true that judicial cognizance can/should be taken of the fact that
230→theft of electricity has become a serious menace and a social evil not only
in the State of U.P. but in the entire country. The electricity has become a
necessity in the present day of society and development of society as well
as nation cannot be conceived of without electricity. The availability of
electricity however is much in deficiency. A huge amount of electricity,
consumed by scrupulous persons is causing a serious loss to public
revenue hampering and obstructing the development of electrical sector in
particular as well as society and nation in general. Therefore, to check
theft of electricity and/or unauthorized use of electricity, stern measures
are required to be taken. The various provisions of Act, 2003 shows that
240→the legislature is also concerned about it and has take several measures
from time to time including making harsh provisions in the statute.
60. However, this by itself would not justify condemnation and
indictment of a citizen or a consumer of electricity by holding him guilty
of unauthorized use of electricity on the vagaries of the officers of
electrical undertaking unless he is disclosed the manner in which he was
found using electricity unauthorizedly on inspection by the officer
concerned and given an opportunity to explain his case, if any. It is well
settled law that no person can be indicted or condemned without giving a
minimal opportunity of hearing. In the case of unauthorized use of
250→electricity found by the assessing officer at any place or the premises etc.
or otherwise, the same has to be disclosed to the person concerned giving
him an opportunity to put his defence. The principles of natural justice

7
WRIC No. - 12783 of 2024
unless excluded by express provision of the Act or by necessary
implication cannot be said to be inapplicable when a citizen or person is
being indicted of a serious charge, i.e., unauthorized use of electricity,
which in some of the cases an offence under Section 135 of Act, 2003.�
260→11.
Learned counsel appearing for the respondent nos.2 and 4, on the
other hand, has contended that even if the inspection team did not find
the petitioner abstracting or consuming electricity at the time of
inspection made on 17.12.2022 and theft can be presumed if any
artificial means or means not authorized by the Board or licencee or
supplier, as the case may be, exists for abstraction or consumption or
usage of electricity by the consumer, until contrary is proved that any
abstraction or consumption or usage of electricity has been dishonestly
caused by such consumer, therefore, the action against the petitioner
270→under Section 135 is justified in view of the proviso to sub-section (1) of
Section 135 of the Act of 2003. It is further contended that in view of
sub-section (5) of Section 126 where the period of unauthorized use of
electricity cannot be ascertained, then assessment of usage can be made
for a period of 12 months immediately preceding date of inspection. In
view of the aforesaid, the action under Section 135 of the Act of 2003
and assessment made under Section 126 of the Act stands justified.   
12.
I have considered the submissions of the counsels for the parties
and perused the record. 
280→13.
The relevant questions to be determined by this Court is (1)
whether in view of the inspection report dated 17.12.2022, theft of
electricity as contemplated under Section 135 of the Act of 2003 is made
out against the petitioner and (2) whether the assessment of electricity
usage, by the respondent no.4, is according to the provisions of Section
126 of the Act of 2003 read with clause 6.8 of the Electricity Supply
Code, 2005. 
14.
The term �unauthorized use of electricity� as defined under
290→Explanation (b) of Section 126 of the Act of 2003 means the usage of
electricity (i) by artificial means; (ii) by means not authorized by
concerned person or authority or licencee; (iii) through a tempered

8
WRIC No. - 12783 of 2024
meter; (iv) for the purpose other than for which the usage of electricity
was authorized and; (v) for the premises or areas other than those for
which the supply of electricity was authorized. In the case in hand,
unauthorized use of electricity is relatable to usage of electricity by any
300→artificial means. 
15.
The perusal of inspection reports dated 28.10.2022 and
08.12.2022, clearly show that there was no evidence to establish
abstraction or consumption of electricity from the energized line on  the
double pole,  going behind the back of the premises of the petitioner. In
the inspection report prepared on 17.12.2022 by visiting the premises of
the petitioner from inside, an 11KV cable is found lying on the floor. The
conclusion of the inspection team is that with the help of artificial means
unauthorized consumption is possible. There is nothing on record to
310→show that any artificial means was available within the premises of the
petitioner, therefore, the presumption of theft, available with the
inspection team, under proviso of sub-section (1) of Section 135 of the
Act of 2003, is misplaced. 
16.
In the absence of any concrete evidence of abstraction or
consumption of unauthorized use of electricity, the action of respondent
no.4, in presuming the act of theft, is based on no evidence as it would
lead to a situation where any electric cable lying in a premises of a
person can indict him for theft on the ground that if he obtains any
320→artificial means, he could unauthorizedly use electricity, which could
never be the intention of the Act of 2003. In the absence of any positive
act of unauthorized use of electricity resorting to artificial means, which
were found on the spot by the inspection team, no presumption can be
drawn. In view of the aforesaid, the allegation of theft and unauthorized
use of electricity under Section 135 of the Act of 2003 is not found to be
established against the petitioner.
17.
The Division Bench judgment of this Court in the case of Ashok
Kumar (supra), has observed that, a huge amount of electricity,
330→consumed by scrupulous persons is causing a serious loss to public

9
WRIC No. - 12783 of 2024
revenue hampering and obstructing the development of electrical sector
in particular as well as society and nation in general. However, this by
itself would not justify condemnation and indictment of a citizen or a
consumer of electricity by holding him guilty of unauthorized use of
electricity on the vagaries of the officers of electrical undertaking unless
he is disclosed the manner in which he was found using electricity
340→unauthorizedly on inspection by the officer concerned and given an
opportunity to explain his case, if any. In view of the aforesaid, in
absence of any positive act of unauthorized use of electricity resorting to
artificial means, which were found on the spot by the inspection team,
no presumption can be drawn that the petitioner was abstracting or
consuming electricity unauthorizedly warranting any penal action.
18.
In view of the fact that the crusher plant of the petitioner had been
directed to be closed down abruptly, under the orders of National Green
Tribunal and the permanent disconnection of electricity had been carried
350→out by the respondent no.4, w.e.f. 12.07.2019, the presence of stone grits
lying in the premises and near the crusher in itself cannot be the basis for
presuming that the crusher plant was being used unauthorizedly by the
petitioner. 
19.
The respondent no.3 while dismissing the appeal of the petitioner
has failed to consider the grounds raised by the petitioner in his appeal.
The observation of respondent no.3 that in the inspection report dated
17.12.2022, it is specifically stated that near the premises of the
petitioner energized 11KV main line is passing by and the jumper is duly
360→connected, is contrary to the report dated 17.12.2022, filed as Annexure-
9 to the writ petition.  
20.
So far as the second issue with regard to assessment of electricity
usage is concerned, in view of the fact that no unauthorized use of
electricity is established against the petitioner, the assessment under
Section 126 of the Act is also unsustainable in the eyes of law. 

10
WRIC No. - 12783 of 2024
370→21.
In view of the aforesaid discussions, the final assessment order
dated 05.07.2023, passed by the respondent no.4, under Section 126 of
the Electricity Act, 2003 and the order of respondent no.3, dated
14.03.2024, dismissing the appeal, cannot be sustained and are hereby
set aside. 
22.
The writ petition stands allowed. No order as to costs.   
(Arun Kumar,J.)
February 27, 2026

1→--- name: pdf description: Read, create, and transform PDF files. Covers pulling text and tables out of PDFs, generating new PDFs, merging and splitting documents, rotating pages, watermarking, encrypting or removing passwords, extracting embedded images, running OCR on scanned documents, and filling out PDF forms including official tax forms. Apply this skill whenever a task involves a .pdf file as input or deliverable. user-invocable: false --- # Working with PDFs Task-oriented recipes for PDF work, built around three Python libraries (`pypdf`, `pdfplumber`, `reportlab`) and the poppler-utils / qpdf command-line suites. 10→ Companion documents in this directory — open them when the task calls for it: - `forms.md` — required reading before filling out any PDF form - `tax.md` — required reading before preparing the official tax forms bundled under `forms/` - `reference.md` — deeper material: pypdfium2 rendering, JavaScript libraries (pdf-lib, pdfjs-dist), advanced qpdf/poppler flags, performance tuning, and troubleshooting ## Choosing a Tool | Goal | Reach for | 20→|------|-----------| | Pull out plain text | `pdfplumber` or `pdftotext` | | Pull out tables | `pdfplumber` (`extract_tables`) | | Combine documents | `pypdf` or `qpdf` | | Break a document apart | `pypdf` (one writer per output) | | Produce a new PDF | `reportlab` (Canvas for absolute layout, Platypus for flowing documents) | | Grab embedded images | `pdfimages` | | Render pages as pictures | `pdftoppm` / `pdf2image` | | OCR a scanned document | `pytesseract` + `pdf2image` | | Fill out a form | see `forms.md` | 30→ ## Getting Content Out of a PDF ### Text ```python import pdfplumber with pdfplumber.open("report.pdf") as doc: full_text = "\n".join(pg.extract_text() or "" for pg in doc.pages) 40→``` From the shell, `pdftotext` is quickest; `-layout` keeps the visual column structure and `-f`/`-l` bound the page range: ```bash pdftotext -layout report.pdf report.txt pdftotext -f 2 -l 4 report.pdf middle_pages.txt ``` ### Tables 50→ `pdfplumber` returns each table as a list of rows; feed them straight into pandas when you need to reshape or export: ```python import pandas as pd import pdfplumber frames = [] with pdfplumber.open("report.pdf") as doc: for pg in doc.pages: 60→ for tbl in pg.extract_tables(): if tbl: frames.append(pd.DataFrame(tbl[1:], columns=tbl[0])) if frames: pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True).to_excel("tables.xlsx", index=False) ``` ### Document Metadata 70→```python from pypdf import PdfReader info = PdfReader("report.pdf").metadata for key in ("title", "author", "subject", "creator"): print(key, "=", getattr(info, key)) ``` ### Embedded Images vs. Page Renders 80→These are different operations — pick the right one: - `pdfimages -all report.pdf img/fig` copies the *original bitmap objects* embedded in the file, untouched by page layout. - `pdftoppm -png -r 300 report.pdf pages/pg` *rasterizes* whole pages — text, vectors, and annotations included — producing what is effectively a screenshot of each page. A rendered page is never a substitute for an extracted image, and vice versa. ### Scanned Documents (OCR) Scanned PDFs contain pictures of text, so extraction tools return nothing useful. Rasterize first, then OCR each page: 90→ ```python # pip install pytesseract pdf2image import pytesseract from pdf2image import convert_from_path pages = convert_from_path("scan.pdf") recognized = [pytesseract.image_to_string(img) for img in pages] print("\n\n".join(recognized)) ``` 100→ ## Reorganizing Pages ### Combine Documents ```python from pypdf import PdfWriter writer = PdfWriter() for path in ["intro.pdf", "body.pdf", "appendix.pdf"]: 110→ writer.append(path) with open("combined.pdf", "wb") as out: writer.write(out) ``` Or from the shell: ```bash qpdf --empty --pages intro.pdf body.pdf appendix.pdf -- combined.pdf 120→``` ### Split into Pieces ```python from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter src = PdfReader("combined.pdf") for idx, pg in enumerate(src.pages, start=1): part = PdfWriter() 130→ part.add_page(pg) with open(f"part_{idx}.pdf", "wb") as out: part.write(out) ``` `qpdf` handles page ranges without any code: ```bash qpdf combined.pdf --pages . 1-5 -- first_five.pdf ``` 140→ ### Rotate ```python from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter src = PdfReader("sideways.pdf") writer = PdfWriter() for pg in src.pages: writer.add_page(pg) 150→writer.pages[0].rotate(90) # clockwise degrees; must be a multiple of 90 with open("upright.pdf", "wb") as out: writer.write(out) ``` ### Stamp a Watermark Overlay one PDF page (the watermark) onto every page of another: 160→```python from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter stamp = PdfReader("stamp.pdf").pages[0] src = PdfReader("contract.pdf") writer = PdfWriter() for pg in src.pages: pg.merge_page(stamp) writer.add_page(pg) 170→ with open("stamped.pdf", "wb") as out: writer.write(out) ``` ### Passwords ```python from pypdf import PdfWriter 180→writer = PdfWriter() writer.append("private.pdf") writer.encrypt(user_password="open-me", owner_password="admin-key") with open("locked.pdf", "wb") as out: writer.write(out) ``` Removing a known password is a one-liner: 190→```bash qpdf --password=open-me --decrypt locked.pdf unlocked.pdf ``` ## Generating PDFs with reportlab Two APIs, two mindsets: - **Canvas** — you place every element at explicit coordinates. The origin is the *bottom-left* corner of the page and y grows upward, so "1 inch from the top" is `page_height - inch - element_height`. - **Platypus** — you build a `story` list of flowables (`Paragraph`, `Table`, `Image`, `Spacer`, `PageBreak`) and the layout engine paginates for you. Prefer this for anything document-like. 200→ ### Minimal Examples ```python from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter from reportlab.pdfgen import canvas c = canvas.Canvas("note.pdf", pagesize=letter) _, page_h = letter c.drawString(72, page_h - 72, "Placed one inch from the top-left corner.") 210→c.line(72, page_h - 90, 400, page_h - 90) c.save() ``` ```python from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet from reportlab.platypus import PageBreak, Paragraph, SimpleDocTemplate, Spacer styles = getSampleStyleSheet() 220→story = [ Paragraph("Annual Summary", styles["Title"]), Spacer(1, 12), Paragraph("Body text flows and wraps automatically. " * 15, styles["Normal"]), PageBreak(), Paragraph("Second Section", styles["Heading1"]), ] SimpleDocTemplate("summary.pdf", pagesize=letter).build(story) ``` 230→### Placing Images Keep the aspect ratio: derive the missing dimension from the source image, or let reportlab do it when fitting a box. ```python from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter from reportlab.lib.units import inch from reportlab.lib.utils import ImageReader from reportlab.pdfgen import canvas 240→c = canvas.Canvas("figure.pdf", pagesize=letter) _, page_h = letter src = ImageReader("chart.png") src_w, src_h = src.getSize() w = 4.5 * inch h = w * src_h / src_w # bottom-left origin: subtract the image height to hang it below the top margin c.drawImage(src, inch, page_h - inch - h, width=w, height=h) 250→c.save() ``` To fit an image inside a fixed region without distortion: ```python c.drawImage("photo.jpg", box_x, box_y, width=box_w, height=box_h, preserveAspectRatio=True, anchor="c") ``` 260→In Platypus, images are flowables — size them yourself and let the engine position them: ```python from reportlab.platypus import Image pic = Image("logo.png", width=w, height=h, hAlign="CENTER") story.append(pic) ``` Prefer `drawImage` over `drawInlineImage`; it registers the image once as a shared object, so repeated use is smaller and faster. 270→ ### Subscripts and Superscripts Do **not** type Unicode sub/superscript characters (₂, ⁹, …) — reportlab's built-in fonts lack those glyphs and they render as black rectangles. Use inline markup inside a `Paragraph` instead: ```python Paragraph("H2O and E = mc2", styles["Normal"]) ``` When drawing directly on a Canvas (no `Paragraph`), simulate the effect by shrinking the font and shifting the baseline manually. 280→ ### Tables Two non-negotiable rules, both consequences of how `Table` lays out cells: 1. **Every cell — headers included — goes inside a `Paragraph`.** Bare strings never wrap; long values run over neighboring cells or off the page. `Paragraph` cells also accept inline markup (``, ``, ``, ``). 2. **Pass explicit `colWidths`, sized by content.** Equal-width columns squeeze prose and waste space on short IDs. Budget most of the printable width (letter with 1" margins ≈ 6.5", landscape ≈ 9") to the prose-heavy columns. ```python from reportlab.lib import colors 290→from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet from reportlab.lib.units import inch from reportlab.platypus import Paragraph, SimpleDocTemplate, Table, TableStyle body = getSampleStyleSheet()["BodyText"] rows = [ [Paragraph("ID", body), Paragraph("Name", body), Paragraph("Notes", body)], [Paragraph("1", body), Paragraph("Widget", body), 300→ Paragraph("Long prose wraps cleanly inside its column instead of spilling over.", body)], ] grid = Table(rows, colWidths=[0.5 * inch, 1.5 * inch, 4.5 * inch], repeatRows=1) grid.setStyle(TableStyle([ ("GRID", (0, 0), (-1, -1), 0.5, colors.grey), ("VALIGN", (0, 0), (-1, -1), "TOP"), ("BACKGROUND", (0, 0), (-1, 0), colors.lightgrey), ])) 310→SimpleDocTemplate("grid.pdf", pagesize=letter).build([grid]) ``` Also: `repeatRows=1` reprints the header when a table crosses a page break; `VALIGN TOP` keeps wrapped rows tidy; and when content is genuinely too wide, switch to `landscape(letter)` rather than shrinking columns into illegibility. ## Always Verify Visually After producing or modifying any PDF — especially after filling form fields, where name-to-label mappings are frequently wrong — render each page and look at it: ```bash 320→pdftoppm -png -r 300 -f 1 -l 1 result.pdf /tmp/check pdftoppm -png -r 300 -f 2 -l 2 result.pdf /tmp/check_p2 ``` pdftoppm appends the page number to the output prefix, so these commands write `/tmp/check-1.png` and `/tmp/check_p2-2.png`. View each PNG and confirm every value sits beside its intended label, nothing overlaps, and nothing is clipped. Inspecting the raw PDF objects cannot catch these problems; rendering does. ## Forms and Tax Forms - Any form-filling task: read `forms.md` first and follow its steps in order. It covers both PDFs with real fillable fields and flat/scanned forms that need positioned text annotations, with helper scripts under `scripts/`. - Tax returns: read `tax.md`. The deliverable is always the official IRS form from `forms/`, filled in — never a homemade summary document. 330→

complete shut down of the crusher plant of the petitioner alongwith all
other crusher plants in the district Chitrakoot, and also directed all other
departments of the State to withdraw all facilities provided to the
petitioner. The officials of the office of respondent no.4 visited the
crusher plant of petitioner on 12.10.2019 and after making inspection
ordered permanent disconnection of electricity supply. Subsequently, the
50→National Green Tribunal modified its earlier order in view of the new
revised guidelines issued by the Government of Uttar Pradesh for re-
starting crusher plants established in district Chitrakoot. In view of the
new guidelines issued on 14.01.2022, inspection of crusher plant of the
petitioner was held by  the U.P. Pollution Control Board on 29.09.2022,
recommending grant of fresh permission to the petitioner to re-start his
plant. 
4.
The officials of the office of respondent no.4 carried out an
inspection of petitioner’s crusher plant on 29.10.2022 for preparing an
60→inspection report in view of the new guidelines issued by the State
Government to re-start the shut crusher plant. In the inspection report
dated 29.10.2022 a note was submitted which stated that, “the consumer
has kept the gate of his premises closed and despite repeated request
refused to open it. Two 11 KV wire is attached to the pole, however,
jumper is not attached, as such, theft of electricity is not ruled out in
future, keeping this in mind, both the 11 KV wire was removed”.
5.
A letter dated 10.11.2022 was issued by the U.P. Pollution Control
Board stating that petitioner is qualifying the minimum required
70→standards for running the crusher plant, pursuant to which, order dated
18.12.2022 was passed permitting the petitioner to re-start his crusher

3
WRIC No. - 12786 of 2024
plant for the period 17.12.2022 to 31.07.2027. The officials of the office
of respondent no.4 again carried out inspection of crusher plant of the
petitioner on 08.12.2022. The inspection report prepared contains a note
that, "at the time of inspection the gate of the premises was found to be
locked,11KV wire was coming from the premises. However, from the
80→rear side of the premises it was found that, no 11KV cable or wire is
connected to the disputed premises”. 
6.
On 17.12.2022, a fresh inspection was held under the supervision
of Junior Engineer alongwith other officials. They entered the premises
of the petitioner's crusher plant and prepared an inspection report, which
contains a note that, "on a confidential information received from the
head office, a joint team made an inspection of the said premises in
which the generator was found in non-working condition. Near the
crusher large amount of stone grits were lying. On the rear side of the
90→premises 11KV line is energized on double pole. An 11KV cable on
whose end three wires are attached was lying on the ground from which
electricity theft can be done. The 11KV cable is connected to the crusher
via transformer, therefore, the consumer by resorting to artificial means
can connect his 11KV cable with energized line and abstract or consume
electricity, which amounts to theft under proviso sub-section (1) of
Section 135 of the Act of 2003. A videography of entire proceedings has
also been done."
7.
On the basis of report dated 17.12.2022, the respondent no.4
100→issued a provisional assessment bill to the petitioner on 22.12.2022,
assessing usage of electricity for a sum of Rs.83,40,994/- with
compounding fee of Rs.15,00,000/-. On the objections filed by the
petitioner, the respondent no.4 passed final assessment order dated
05.07.2023. In final assessment, the amount assessed was reduced to
Rs.62,34,761 and compounding fee was quantified as Rs.28,00,000/-.
The petitioner challenged the final assessment dated 05.07.2023 in Writ-
C No.26481 of 2023, which was disposed of on the ground of alternative
remedy of appeal under Section 127 of the Act of 2003. The petitioner

110→4
WRIC No. - 12786 of 2024
challenged the final assessment in appeal before the respondent no.3,
which has been dismissed by the order dated 14.03.2024. Thus
aggrieved, the petitioner is before this Court.
8.
It is contended by the learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner
that under the provisions of Section 135 of the Act of 2003, whoever
dishonestly taps, makes or causes to be made in connection with
overhead, underground or under water lines or cables or service wires or
120→service facilities of a licencee or supplier, as the case may be, so as to
abstract or consume electricity shall be punishable with imprisonment.
Therefore, unless and until electricity is abstracted or consumed or used,
prosecution under Section 135 of the Act cannot be initiated against the
petitioners. The reports prepared by the officials of respondent no.4 on
29.10.2022 and 08.12.2022 does not show that any electricity was being
abstracted, consumed or used by the petitioner, except for the
observation in the report dated 29.10.2022 that there exists possibility of
theft in future. It is further contended that the inspection report dated
17.12.2022 refers possibility of theft through artificial means, however,
130→neither the petitioner was found consuming electricity, nor there was any
artificial means available in the premises of the petitioner, which could
have been used for abstracting or consuming electricity running from the
double pole behind the premises of the petitioner.
9.
Learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner has further stated that in
the absence of any positive act of abstraction or consumption of
electricity by resorting to any artificial means as mentioned in Section
135 of the Act of 2003, the allegation of theft of electricity is not
established, as such, no demand under Section 126 of the Act could have
140→been made against the petitioner. It is further submitted that even if it is
assumed that the petitioner could have abstracted or consumed electricity
with help of artificial means, the assessment of electricity usage as
quantified in the final assessment order dated 05.07.2023 for a period of
365 days is unsustainable, in view of the fact that in the report prepared
by the officials of respondent no.4 on 08.12.2022, there is a clear

5
WRIC No. - 12786 of 2024
observation that no 11KV cable or wire is attached to the double pole
150→energized line, therefore, possibility of theft, even if accepted, could
have been only with effect from 09.12.2022. 
10.
Learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner further argues that in
view of the order passed by the National Green Tribunal, the production
and sale of stone grits was completely banned w.e.f. 22.06.2018. The
stone grits found near the crusher plant was the stock lying with the
petitioner when the crusher plant was abruptly stopped and the petitioner
was directed to suspend his business. He further contends that the entire
proceedings against the petitioner under Section 126 read with Section
160→135 of the Act of 2003 is on basis of presumption. 
11.
Learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner in support of his
contentions has relied upon a Division Bench judgment of this Court in
the case of Ashok Kumar and others vs. State of U.P. and other
reported in 2008 (6) ADJ 660. Paragraph nos.56 to 60 of the aforesaid
judgment are relied upon and are reproduced hereinafter:-
“56. The provisional assessment notices are in question in all these cases
except writ petitions no. 21986 of 2008 and 22356 of 2008 and have also
been challenged on the ground that neither they have been issued
170→observing the procedure prescribed under Section 126 of the Act, 2007
read with Clause 6.8 of Code, 2005 nor the petitioners have been given
adequate opportunity of defence.
57. Sub-section 1 of Section 126 provides that if on inspection, the
assessing authority comes to the conclusion that the person concerned is
indulged in unauthorized user of electricity, the assessing officer shall
provisionally assess, to best of its judgment, electricity charges payable
by that person or by any other person benefited by such use. Therefore,
the conditions precedent to attract the power of assessment under Section
126 (1) is the conclusion drawn by the assessing officer that the person
180→concerned has indulged in unauthorized use of electricity.
58. The term "unauthorized use of electricity" is defined in explanation
(b) to Section 126 which includes usage of electricity (i) by any artificial
means; or (b) by a means not authorised by the concerned person or
authority or licensee; or (iii) through a tampered meter; or (iv) for the
purpose other than for which the usage of electricity was authorised.
Before issuing an assessment notice, therefore, the assessing officer must
record its conclusion that the person concerned or any other person
benefited has used electricity unauthorizedly in terms as defined in
Explanation (b) of Section 126. The Act in respect to the stage of
190→recording of conclusion by assessing officer regarding user of electricity
by the person unauthorizedly does not provide specifically for any
opportunity of hearing to the person concerned but also simultaneously

6
WRIC No. - 12786 of 2024
does not prohibit the same. The allegation of unauthorised use of
electricity by a person concerned, as defined in Explanation (b) also
covers within its ambit certain acts/omission which constitute an offence
under Section 135 of the Act, 2003. Therefore, it is a serious matter and
200→no person can be indicted and held guilty of user of electricity
unauthorizedly unless he is given an opportunity of hearing before
coming to such conclusion. Where a person is held guilty of unauthorised
user of electricity, besides making him responsible for paying penalty in
the shape of assessment under the Act, 2003 it also causes stigma on his
conduct. He is declared an anti-social person indulging in a serious
unsocial activity, by causing loss to the society and country in general and
electricity undertaking in particular. Such condemnation of a person
would not be permissible on the mere vagaries of the authority i.e.
assessing officer unless such a person is given a fair opportunity of
210→hearing i.e. putting his defence before the said authority. This Court is
clearly of the view that before making provisional assessment, the
assessing officer, in law, is bound to afford an opportunity to the
consumer or person concerned of the allegations of means and ways in
which he is said to have unauthorizedly used electricity, and, should be
given an opportunity of placing his defence. Thereafter the assessing
officer shall record its conclusion with respect to unauthorised use of
electricity, to confer upon himself the jurisdiction to issue provisional
assessment notice. The object of opportunity at the two stages namely,
before arriving at the conclusion of unauthorised use of electricity and
220→before making final assessment are distinct. In the former, it is the very
issue whether the consumer is guilty of unauthorised use of electricity or
not and in later case it is the quantum of amount which he is required to
pay as a compensation and a fiscal preventive measure for committing
such irregularity. The first one is the stage of finding the person guilty and
later one is the stage of determining extent of monetary liability for
compensating electrical undertaking qua the alleged unauthorised use of
electricity by such persons. It is only when the proceedings are conducted
in the above manner, the assessment made can be held valid and not
otherwise.
230→59. It is true that judicial cognizance can/should be taken of the fact that
theft of electricity has become a serious menace and a social evil not only
in the State of U.P. but in the entire country. The electricity has become a
necessity in the present day of society and development of society as well
as nation cannot be conceived of without electricity. The availability of
electricity however is much in deficiency. A huge amount of electricity,
consumed by scrupulous persons is causing a serious loss to public
revenue hampering and obstructing the development of electrical sector in
particular as well as society and nation in general. Therefore, to check
theft of electricity and/or unauthorized use of electricity, stern measures
240→are required to be taken. The various provisions of Act, 2003 shows that
the legislature is also concerned about it and has take several measures
from time to time including making harsh provisions in the statute.
60. However, this by itself would not justify condemnation and
indictment of a citizen or a consumer of electricity by holding him guilty
of unauthorized use of electricity on the vagaries of the officers of
electrical undertaking unless he is disclosed the manner in which he was
found using electricity unauthorizedly on inspection by the officer
concerned and given an opportunity to explain his case, if any. It is well
settled law that no person can be indicted or condemned without giving a
250→minimal opportunity of hearing. In the case of unauthorized use of
electricity found by the assessing officer at any place or the premises etc.

7
WRIC No. - 12786 of 2024
or otherwise, the same has to be disclosed to the person concerned giving
him an opportunity to put his defence. The principles of natural justice
unless excluded by express provision of the Act or by necessary
implication cannot be said to be inapplicable when a citizen or person is
being indicted of a serious charge, i.e., unauthorized use of electricity,
260→which in some of the cases an offence under Section 135 of Act, 2003.”
12.
Learned counsel appearing for the respondent nos.2 and 4, on the
other hand, has contended that even if the inspection team did not find
the petitioner abstracting or consuming electricity at the time of
inspection made on 17.12.2022 and theft can be presumed if any
artificial means or means not authorized by the Board or licencee or
supplier, as the case may be, exists for abstraction or consumption or
usage of electricity by the consumer, until contrary is proved that any
abstraction or consumption or usage of electricity has been dishonestly
270→caused by such consumer, therefore, the action against the petitioner
under Section 135 is justified in view of the proviso to sub-section (1) of
Section 135 of the Act of 2003. It is further contended that in view of
sub-section (5) of Section 126 where the period of unauthorized use of
electricity cannot be ascertained, then assessment of usage can be made
for a period of 12 months immediately preceding date of inspection. In
view of the aforesaid, the action under Section 135 of the Act of 2003
and assessment made under Section 126 of the Act stands justified.   
13.
I have considered the submissions of the counsels for the parties
280→and perused the record. 
14.
The relevant questions to be determined by this Court is (1)
whether in view of the inspection report dated 17.12.2022, theft of
electricity as contemplated under Section 135 of the Act of 2003 is made
out against the petitioner and (2) whether the assessment of electricity
usage, by the respondent no.4, is according to the provisions of Section
126 of the Act of 2003 read with clause 6.8 of the Electricity Supply
Code, 2005. 
15.
290→The term “unauthorized use of electricity” as defined under
Explanation (b) of Section 126 of the Act of 2003 means the usage of
electricity (i) by artificial means; (ii) by means not authorized by

8
WRIC No. - 12786 of 2024
concerned person or authority or licencee; (iii) through a tempered
meter; (iv) for the purpose other than for which the usage of electricity
was authorized and; (v) for the premises or areas other than those for
which the supply of electricity was authorized. In the case in hand,
300→unauthorized use of electricity is relatable to usage of electricity by any
artificial means. 
16.
The perusal of inspection reports dated 29.10.2022 and
08.12.2022, clearly show that there was no evidence to establish
abstraction or consumption of electricity from the energized line on  the
double pole,  going behind the back of the premises of the petitioner. In
the inspection report prepared on 17.12.2022 by visiting the premises of
the petitioner from inside, an 11KV cable is found lying on the floor. The
conclusion of the inspection team is that with the help of artificial means
310→unauthorized consumption is possible. There is nothing on record to
show that any artificial means was available within the premises of the
petitioner, therefore, the presumption of theft, available with the
inspection team, under proviso of sub-section (1) of Section 135 of the
Act of 2003, is misplaced. 
17.
In the absence of any concrete evidence of abstraction or
consumption of unauthorized use of electricity, the action of respondent
no.4, in presuming the act of theft, is based on no evidence as it would
lead to a situation where any electric cable lying in a premises of a
320→person can indict him for theft on the ground that if he obtains any
artificial means, he could unauthorizedly use electricity, which could
never be the intention of the Act of 2003. In the absence of any positive
act of unauthorized use of electricity resorting to artificial means, which
were found on the spot by the inspection team, no presumption can be
drawn. In view of the aforesaid, the allegation of theft and unauthorized
use of electricity under Section 135 of the Act of 2003 is not found to be
established against the petitioner.
18.
The Division Bench judgment of this Court in the case of Ashok
330→Kumar (supra), has observed that, a huge amount of electricity,

9
WRIC No. - 12786 of 2024
consumed by scrupulous persons is causing a serious loss to public
revenue hampering and obstructing the development of electrical sector
in particular as well as society and nation in general. However, this by
itself would not justify condemnation and indictment of a citizen or a
consumer of electricity by holding him guilty of unauthorized use of
electricity on the vagaries of the officers of electrical undertaking unless
340→he is disclosed the manner in which he was found using electricity
unauthorizedly on inspection by the officer concerned and given an
opportunity to explain his case, if any. In view of the aforesaid, in
absence of any positive act of unauthorized use of electricity, resorting to
artificial means, which were found on the spot by the inspection team,
no presumption can be drawn that the petitioner was abstracting or
consuming electricity unauthorizedly warranting any penal action.
19.
In view of the fact that the crusher plant of the petitioner had been
directed to be closed down abruptly, under the orders of National Green
350→Tribunal and the permanent disconnection of electricity had been carried
out by the respondent no.4, w.e.f. 12.10.2019, the presence of stone grits
lying in the premises and near the crusher in itself cannot be the basis for
presuming that the crusher plant was being used unauthorizedly by the
petitioner. 
20.
The respondent no.3 while dismissing the appeal of the petitioner
has failed to consider the grounds raised by the petitioner in his appeal.
The observation of respondent no.3 that in the inspection report dated
17.12.2022, it is specifically stated that near the premises of the
360→petitioner energized 11KV main line is passing by and the jumper is duly
connected, is contrary to the report dated 17.12.2022, filed as Annexure-
9 to the writ petition.  
21.
So far as the second issue with regard to assessment of electricity
usage is concerned, in view of the fact that no unauthorized use of
electricity is established against the petitioner, the assessment under
Section 126 of the Act is also unsustainable in the eyes of law. 

10
370→WRIC No. - 12786 of 2024
22.
In view of the aforesaid discussions, the final assessment order
dated 05.07.2023, passed by the respondent no.4, under Section 126 of
the Electricity Act, 2003 and the order of respondent no.3, dated
14.03.2024, dismissing the appeal, cannot be sustained and are hereby
set aside. 
23.
The writ petition stands allowed. No order as to costs.   
(Arun Kumar,J.)
380→February 27, 2026
Ashok Kr.
Digitally signed by :- 
ASHOK KUMAR 
High Court of Judicature at Allahabad

summary.text:
This is a companion to SCJ-285 (Sangam Crusher Works). Same judge, same date, same pattern, different crusher:
**Facts**

M/s K.G.N. Stone Crusher Mill (and its proprietor) held a 140 kW / 11 kV connection in Chitrakoot. Production was stopped after an NGT/UPPCB shutdown of crushers on 22.06.2018, and the licensee permanently disconnected the supply 12.10.2019. After revised State guidelines, UPPCB inspected on 29.10.2022 and later permitted restart from 17.12.2022 to 31.07.2027. Restart-related inspections on 08.12.

50→- **facts**: 1–2 short paragraphs (about 80–180 words) of the story — who, the connection,

  (cream box). Labels print as ordinary words (Headnote / Factual Summary), not letter-spaced.
- **holding_units[]**: `{provision, code, clause, topic, type, question?, holding,
  qualifier?, paras, flag?}`. Do **not** write `limiting_facts` (dropped from the digest;
  the story belongs in `facts`). `provision` is the key, e.g. `UP-2005::4.3(f)`, `EA2003::56(2)`,

  multi-state scope. `paras` = judgment paragraph pins.

summary.text:
I have good numbers. Let me think through the token economics clearly.
The token cost for ordinary 1-2 page cases is dominated by the catalog (≈4.3 k tokens) and the example (≈1.3 k tokens) that get re-sent on every turn. A typical 1-page case still needs 6–8 turns, so those two files alone can add 35–45 k tokens of repeated context—most of the waste.

You can cut that dramatically without losing anything important by adding a “short-case” gate right after the ticket is read:

1. If pages ≤ 2 and words < 800, switch to short path:
   • Skip the full catalog; instead 1) grep the catalog for every clause number that appears in the judgment, 2) load only the matching provisions (usually 1–3 sections), 3) use a 15-line skeleton instead of the 50-line SCJ-280 example.  
   • Keep the same JSON schema—nothing is dropped (facts, holding, provision key, flag, not_decided, authorities).  
   • Prompt the model to read ticket + judgment + fp in one go, then write JSON; max 15 turns.

2. For significant cases keep the original full-catalog path.

content:
Most of the money on a 1–2 page ordinary order is **not the judgment**. It is the same fixed load you pay on a 10-page significant case, then re-billed every tool turn.

**What the JSON step actually reads today** (rough chars/4):

| Input | 1-page ordinary (SCJ-287) | 10-page significant (SCJ-285) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Judgment `.txt` | ~400 | ~5,500 |
| `catalog.txt` (every case) | ~4,300 | ~4,300 |
| Example `SCJ-280.json` | ~1,300 | ~1,300 |
| JSON you write | ~900 | ~2,300 |

On SCJ-287 the order is **236 words**. Catalog + example are ~**10×** that. `finalize_scj.py` (PDF, index, git) is free of model tokens. `jurisprudence/index.json` is already correctly kept out of the authoring step.

Turns multiply this. A short case still does: ticket → txt → fp → catalog → example → write JSON → finalize. Each later turn resends earlier file dumps. So a 1-pager is cheaper than a 10-pager, but **not 10× cheaper**. Catalog is the flat tax.

Significance does not help as a gate. The model only classifies after it has already read the case. Page count and word count are already on the ticket **before** Grok starts. Use those.

**What not to cut** (this is the “don’t lose anything important” list):

- Identity, disposition, `page_count`, `significance`
- Headnote (the rule, even if one sentence)
- Factual summary (short is fine)
- One keyed holding (`CODE::clause`) and paragraph pins
- `flag` when the court names the wrong/ambiguous clause (SCJ-287’s 4.4 vs 4.44 is exactly that)
- `not_decided[]` when something was raised and left open
- Every real citation, if any
- PDF + commit + push

Those are the spine. Cutting them would lose jurisprudence, not tokens.

**Where you can save without losing that:**

1. **Short path on the ticket, not on significance.** If `page_count ≤ 2` or `word_count < ~800`, do not load the whole catalog or SCJ-280. Grep `catalog.txt` for clause numbers that actually appear in the order. Use a 15-line skeleton instead of SCJ-280. Significant 2-pagers still get a full record; they just don’t swallow 4k unused keys.

2. **Fewer turns on the short path.** Prompt: read ticket + txt + fp, write JSON, finalize. No extra greps of the judgment, no re-read of the JSON. Cap `--max-turns` around 15. Quality lives in the files, not in extra turns.

3. **Shorter prose, same nodes.** Ordinary JSON can drop the restated “Question”, keep one holding unit, keep facts to ~60–90 words, and skip a principle tag that only repeats the holding. Do **not** skip the provision key, flag, or `not_decided`.

4. **Do not batch, and do not use a weaker model for the JSON.** Batching truncates; a cheaper model is where 4.4/4.44 and “possibility of theft” flags die. The save is input + turns, not a dumber author.

5. **Do not skip PDF/git.** That is not where tokens go.

A realistic 1–2 page ordinary case then costs roughly **catalog+example+turns**, not “another SCJ-285”. You should see something like **half or better** versus today’s short-case bill, with the same nodes on the spine.

If you want, I can wire the ticket gate (`page_count` / `word_count` → compact prompt, no full catalog) and leave the long/significant path unchanged.

content:
A **turn** is one model call: Grok thinks, then either writes text or uses a tool. The next turn is a **new** call that resends the system prompt **plus everything already read**. That is why a 236-word order is not cheap just because it is short.

Typical JSON-only case (the unattended loop, not this chat):

1. Read the ticket  
2. Read the judgment  
3. Read the fingerprint  
4. Read the whole catalog  
5. Read the SCJ-280 example  
6. Write the JSON  
7. Run finalize  

That is about **7–10 turns**. `--max-turns 50` is only a ceiling. SCJ-284 (253 words) still took **~2 minutes** of Grok, not because the order was long, but because of those steps.

Each turn’s bill is roughly:

`system prompt + tools + all files already dumped + the new step`

So catalog (~4,300 tokens) loaded on turn 4 is paid again on turns 5, 6, 7… The judgment on a 1-pager is ~400 tokens; by then catalog has already drowned it.

**What we would change** (short path only: ≤2 pages or ≲800 words):

- Do not load the full catalog; grep the clause that is actually in the order  
- Do not load SCJ-280; use a tiny skeleton  
- 3–5 turns: ticket + judgment → write JSON → finalize  
- Same nodes: headnote, facts, keyed holding, flag, not_decided, citations if any  
- Long/significant cases stay as they are  

**Estimated save** (JSON-authoring tokens, vs today’s short-case path):

| Case type | Share of the queue | Likely save |

| 1–2 page ordinary / procedural | most remaining UP writs | **about 40–60%** |
